FlameSafe turns NASA's microgravity combustion research into fire-safety evidence for future habitats, which will breathe more oxygen at lower pressure than the ISS. We summarize 24 PSI investigations and 660 ISS flame tests through a reproducible pipeline where every number traces back to its NASA file; we rank the investigations with transparent, editable criteria; and we interpret them with survival models. Key results: each +5 points of oxygen cuts the risk of self-extinction by about 81% (HR 0.19); a four-term physical law predicts burn duration (C-index 0.89) and transfers to an unseen fuel and campaign (0.93); flames near exploration air lasted a median of 62.5 s vs 9 s near ISS cabin air; and flame shrinking warns of extinction 5-10 s ahead. No normal flame has been tested near lunar-base air, and none in partial gravity, so those values are labeled as bounds and the missing experiments are named. Every reading shows its evidence level, and a Gemini assistant answers only from cited, reviewed sources. Designers can compare habitat atmospheres, prioritize detection and suppression, and choose the next experiment to fly. Open and versioned, the pipeline scales to new PSI campaigns.
details:
What it does. FlameSafe turns NASA’s microgravity combustion research into fire-safety evidence for future space habitats. Lunar and Martian habitats are planned with more oxygen at lower pressure than the ISS cabin, a combination that has barely been tested. FlameSafe answers three questions for any habitat air: how long does a flame keep burning, how likely is it to still be burning after 30 or 60 seconds, and how much evidence stands behind that number?

How it works. A reproducible pipeline ingests 24 combustion investigations and 660 ISS gas-flame tests from NASA Physical Sciences Informatics. Raw files stay immutable, missing values stay missing instead of becoming zeros, and every number traces back to its NASA source file. We re-derived each flame’s end from sensor time series (99.6% agreement with NASA’s labels) and measured flames in ISS video on Google Cloud (Spearman 0.97 against the published tables). Survival models treat flames whose fuel was cut as censored rather than discarding them. Our burn-time law uses four physical groups: flame temperature, pressure, fuel flow and flame position. It ranks held-out flames with a C-index of 0.89 and transfers to a fuel and campaign it never saw (0.93). Each extra 5 points of oxygen cuts the risk of self-extinction by about 81%. A multi-criteria ranking orders the 24 investigations by their value for fire safety.

Benefits and impact. Mission designers can compare candidate habitat atmospheres, see where detection and suppression matter most, and choose the next experiment to fly. Every reading carries an evidence level: measured nearby, model interpolation, or no number at all. The data gaps are explicit: no normal flame has been tested near lunar-base air, and no flame has been tested in partial gravity. We also found that a flame visibly shrinks 5-10 seconds before it goes out on its own, a signal a simple camera could watch.

Tools. Python with pandas, DuckDB, lifelines, statsmodels, scikit-learn, SciPy, Cantera for thermochemistry and OpenCV for video. A FastAPI evidence service runs on Google Cloud Run, with Cloud Storage, Cloud Build, Secret Manager and Firestore behind it. Gemini writes the answers in our “Ask” assistant over BM25 retrieval. The web app uses Next.js, React and TypeScript with interactive charts, hosted on Vercel. All code is open on GitHub. No custom hardware was used.

Creativity. We derived model inputs from combustion physics, and the resulting law holds on a campaign it never saw. We processed ISS operations video to measure the flames, and we publish our negative results, such as soot glow fading failing as a warning sign. The AI assistant may only quote reviewed sources and rejects any number it cannot find in them.

Factors considered. Scientific honesty first. We never mix incomparable variables, and lunar and Martian values are labeled as bounds because no partial-gravity data exist. A physics reviewer approved every finding. Beyond that, we weighed reproducibility, a free-tier cloud budget, accessibility and bilingual use (English and Spanish), and a clear executive dashboard for decision makers.
